source.title: Random Feature Amplification: Feature Learning and Generalization in Neural Networks
source.authors: Spencer Frei; Niladri S. Chatterji; P. Bartlett

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes and experimentally measures noisy-label learning on a synthetic XOR cluster distribution, rather than randomly relabeled images as in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a theoretical result and Figure 2 experiments on adversarial or 15% flipped labels in a synthetic XOR task. It does not test completely random labels, unstructured inputs, explicit regularization, or learning order. Figure 1 and results cited from other work are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: The synthetic XOR setting provides results on learning shared signal before memorizing noise (V6), and on interpolation with partial label corruption (a component of V4). Early stopping does not establish failure to fit noisy labels eventually.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors prove that early-stopped gradient descent learns useful features and achieves classification error close to the noise rate on their XOR distribution. Their experiments show that subsequent noise fitting preserves optimal test accuracy in high dimensions but reduces test accuracy in low dimensions.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic XOR cluster distribution rather than images; two-layer ReLU network with only first-layer weights trained and fixed second-layer weights; theoretical arbitrary label corruption plus experiments with 15% flips; early stopping is required for the main guarantee.
record.method_sensitivity: The post-interpolation test behavior differs between the n ≫ d and d ≫ n regimes.
record.problems: The main theorem applies to a specific synthetic XOR distribution under restrictive assumptions and uses early stopping. Figure 2 reports qualitative curve behavior without exact plotted values or uncertainty. The reported label-noise fraction in the experiments is 15%, not a sweep over corruption levels.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 is an illustrative decision-boundary plot and does not add a separately reported result beyond Theorem 3.1. Cited results from prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, chance test performance, and fitting with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or unstructured Gaussian-noise inputs. Gaussian variation around informative cluster centers is not this test.

Perfect training fit throughout a sweep from zero to complete random labeling, and steadily increasing test error across that sweep. Interpolation with retained signal is established only at 15% corruption in the high-dimensional experiment.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and removing those regularizers.
Direct comparison of wholly real versus wholly random datasets; learning order beyond the tested synthetic XOR setting.

record.verdict_notes: Neither early stopping nor the contrast in post-overfitting accuracy challenges eventual memorization or a trend across corruption fractions. Test labels are also corrupted, so 85% accuracy is the reported optimal level at 15% noise. The supplied text supports qualitative trajectories but does not expose readable plotted curve coordinates.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling of training images; zero or near-zero training error with test error at chance; unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence as the corrupted-label fraction varies.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from no corruption to all labels corrupted, and steady test-error rise across that full range. The theorem allows arbitrary adversarial corruption; Figure 2 uses 15% flipped labels.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, and whether these are learned differently over training.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network
rows.size_stated: m neurons; width otherwise described as essentially constant
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on logistic loss, training first-layer weights while second-layer weights remain fixed; early-stopped at T = 1 + 1/(4α) iterations.

conditions.value: Constant fraction η of labels corrupted arbitrarily
Random initialization with sufficiently small variance; step-size α under assumptions (A1)–(A7)

rows.measure: Training classification on clean and noisy training points; population test classification error.
rows.value: With probability at least 1 − 4δ, all clean training points are classified correctly and all noisy training points incorrectly; test error ≤ η + C√(log(1/δ)/n).
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − 4δ; bound includes C√(log(1/δ)/n).
rows.note: The result explicitly leaves noisy training points misclassified, so the training set is not fit perfectly. The theoretical noise is arbitrary adversarial corruption, not necessarily random.
rows.check: The theorem establishes an early stage where every clean training label is fitted and every corrupted training label is rejected. This bears on V6, not a challenge to V4's eventual interpolation claim. The theorem alone does not establish subsequent memorization. Noise is bounded by a sufficiently small constant under (A4), rather than an unrestricted constant fraction.
